<reason>A close, well-fought debate. CON built a genuinely sharp frame ("either the benefit is tiny or the cost is real," then "unnecessary where it works, useless where needed," then the insurance metaphor) and landed clever turns: EBT as a government-issued substitute for the prepaid card, and the networked bill acceptor dying in the same outage. But PRO answered the central dilemma with a coherent third option (small real cost, guarantee rather than favor), pressed the woman who qualifies for no benefits, and in the closing caught CON's B4.3 admission that "a targeted rule would follow" once refusal actually occurs — reframing CON as disputing timing, not principle. PRO also exposed a real tension: CON spends the whole debate explaining why rational retailers drop cash, then relies on competition ensuring someone always keeps it. CON's holdout-captures-customers reply is plausible but does not address local lockouts or the conceded principle. PRO's two clipped turns are a real execution cost, and CON was more disciplined, which keeps this a razor-thin edge rather than a clear win.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's closing seizure of CON's "a targeted rule would follow... fire codes answered real fires" [B4.3], recasting it as a concession to the mandate's principle and pairing it with the contradiction between CON's cost case (retailers rationally abandon cash) and CON's promise that they never fully will.</best_rebuttal>
